report:
## Conclusion: The claim is **not supported by human clinical evidence**

Capsaicin shows promising anti-cancer activity **in laboratory settings** (cell cultures and animal models), but there is **no clinical evidence** that it treats breast cancer in humans. The claim is therefore premature and not currently supported.

### What the evidence shows

**In vitro and animal studies:** Multiple studies demonstrate that capsaicin inhibits proliferation and induces apoptosis (programmed cell death) in breast cancer cell lines such as MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231, through mechanisms including cell-cycle arrest, modulation of the EGFR/HER-2 pathway, and NF-κB down-regulation ([Dovepress](https://www.dovepress.com/capsaicin-inhibits-proliferation-and-induces-apoptosis-in-breast-cance-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DDDT); [Nature Oncogene](https://www.nature.com/articles/onc2009335.pdf)). A comprehensive review concluded capsaicin has anticancer properties across multiple cancer types, but noted that further clinical studies are needed to understand efficacy and safety in humans ([Anticancer Research](https://ar.iiarjournals.org/content/36/3/837)).

**No human clinical trials for breast cancer treatment:** A 2023 review in PMC stated that "the clinical value of per os capsaicin to complement chemotherapy is still speculative" ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/)). Snopes fact-checked the claim that spicy peppers can cure breast cancer and rated it as far from certain, noting challenges such as delivering capsaicin to tumor sites ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/)).

**Conflicting evidence:** One study found that capsaicin-induced inactivation of sensory neurons may actually promote a *more aggressive* gene expression phenotype in breast cancer cells ([Springer](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10549-006-9219-7)).

**Current human use:** Capsaicin is clinically used only topically for pain management, including chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy in breast cancer patients ([Frontiers](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2024.1452099/full))—not as a cancer treatment.

### Bottom line
While capsaicin is a promising candidate for future research, it has not been proven to treat breast cancer in humans. No clinical trials have tested it as a breast cancer therapy, and delivery challenges remain significant.
